const ok = t => new URL(t, base).hostname.endsWith('good.example');

questions.prompt: What pathname does this code log?

A relative reference replaces the last base segment (go), it does not append beneath it.

questions.prompt: What href does this code log?

Two ../ steps apply: one pops account after the last segment (settings) is dropped.
The href IDL attribute returns the resolved absolute URL, not the raw content attribute.

questions.prompt: Does the resolved host stay app.example.com after this normalizer runs?

hostname strips the port and equals app.example.com exactly.

const u = new URL('https://app.example.com:8443/next', 'https://app.example.com/');
console.log([u.hostname === 'app.example.com', u.origin === 'https://app.example.com'].join(','));

questions.prompt: What does this snippet log?

choices.rationale: The raw string begins with a tab, so startsWith('//') is false and the guard never fires.
The tab is stripped, not percent-encoded, and the // then starts an authority instead of a path.
After whitespace removal the input is protocol-relative, so the host is replaced rather than kept.

query.title: Leading control characters are stripped before parsing

questions.prompt: What href does this code log?

A dot is in the urlencoded safe set and is left as-is.

questions.prompt: Does this hostname check accept the userinfo-style target as the allowed host?

questions.prompt: Which source list governs an load under this policy?

That is style-src, which covers stylesheets, not images.
No directive here is 'none'; img-src falls back to default-src, which is 'self'.

<script>alert(1)</script>

questions.rationale: A nonce or hash source in script-src makes 'unsafe-inline' be ignored, so an inline script with no nonce is blocked rather than allowed.

questions.prompt: How many of these script loads are allowed when both policies are enforced?

query.title: Multiple policies intersect

questions.prompt: Does this policy block a form submission to https://evil.example?

<form action="https://evil.example/collect" method="post">

query.title: form-action has no default-src fallback

questions.rationale: form-action does not inherit from default-src, so default-src 'none' leaves form submissions completely unrestricted.

www.example.com is a different host, and 'self' never implies subdomains.
Port 8443 is not the page's port, so the origin does not match.

questions.prompt: How many of these URLs match the host source https://*.example.com?

https://example.com has no subdomain label, so *.example.com does not cover the bare domain.

questions.prompt: How many cookies does the jar hold after these three Set-Cookie headers?

choices.rationale: Only cookies sharing name, domain AND path overwrite each other; the /admin cookie is stored separately.
The third header has the same name, domain and path as the first, so it replaces it instead of adding a new entry.
Only three headers were sent, so the jar can never hold four cookies.

Set-Cookie: a=1; Path=/
Set-Cookie: a=2; Path=/admin
Set-Cookie: a=3; Path=/

query.explanation: A stored cookie is keyed by the triple (name, domain, path), not by name alone. 'a' on Path=/ and 'a' on Path=/admin are two distinct cookies, while the third header overwrites the first because it shares the same name, domain and path. The jar ends up with two entries.
query.title: Cookie identity is name + domain + path

questions.prompt: What Cookie header does a request to /a/b/c send from this jar?

choices.rationale: Cookies are not ordered by creation time first; path length decides the order.
This is ascending path length; the longest matching path is sent first, not last.
/a/b is longer than /a, so id=2 precedes id=3.

stored, in creation order:
  id=1  Path=/
  id=2  Path=/a/b
  id=3  Path=/a

query.explanation: All three cookies path-match /a/b/c. The Cookie header lists matching cookies with longer paths first, and ties are broken by earlier creation time. So /a/b comes first, then /a, then /. Servers that read only the first occurrence of a name can therefore be steered by a cookie set on a deeper path.
query.title: Cookie header ordering by path length

questions.prompt: Which host does this cookie's Domain attribute not match?

choices.rationale: An exact host match always satisfies the Domain attribute.
Domain=example.com covers every subdomain, so this host receives the cookie.
Deeper subdomains still end with '.example.com', so the cookie is sent.

query.explanation: Domain=example.com matches the exact host and any host that ends with '.example.com', so example.com, api.example.com and a.b.example.com all receive the cookie. notexample.com shares the text suffix but not a dot boundary, so it is a different registrable host and never gets the cookie.
query.title: Domain matching is suffix plus dot boundary

questions.prompt: What value does a cookie parser store for this header?

choices.rationale: Splitting on every '=' and keeping one field discards the rest of the value, which the spec keeps intact.
The value starts right after the first '=', so it begins with 'a'.
The value runs to the first ';', so the trailing '=c' is included.

query.explanation: The name/value pair is split at the first '=' only; every remaining character up to the first ';' belongs to the value. So the name is 't' and the value is the literal 'a=b=c'. Hand-written parsers that split on every '=' corrupt such values and can be tricked into reading attacker-chosen names.
query.title: Only the first '=' separates name from value

questions.prompt: How many of these headers are rejected by cookie prefix rules on https?

choices.rationale: The first header carries a __Secure- name with no Secure attribute, which is always rejected.
Two headers break the rules: the missing Secure in header 1 and the missing explicit Path=/ in header 3.
Domain is allowed with __Secure-, so header 4 is accepted and only two are rejected.

questions.code:
Set-Cookie: __Secure-a=1; Path=/
Set-Cookie: __Host-b=2; Path=/; Secure
Set-Cookie: __Host-c=3; Secure
Set-Cookie: __Secure-d=4; Secure; Domain=example.com

query.explanation: __Secure- only demands the Secure attribute, so header 1 fails (no Secure) but header 4 passes even with Domain. __Host- demands Secure, Path=/ and no Domain: header 2 passes, header 3 fails because its default path is not the required explicit Path=/. Two headers are rejected.
query.title: __Secure- vs __Host- requirements

questions.prompt: Which cross-site request carries this cookie?

choices.rationale: POST is not a safe method, so Lax withholds the cookie even on a top-level navigation.
An iframe is a subresource load, not a top-level navigation, so Lax cookies are omitted.

choices.text: a cross-site fetch with credentials included
choices.rationale: credentials: 'include' cannot override SameSite; a cross-site fetch is not a top-level navigation.

questions.code: Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Lax

query.explanation: SameSite=Lax attaches the cookie to cross-site requests only when they are top-level navigations using a safe method such as GET. Cross-site POST submissions, subresource and iframe loads, and credentialed fetch/XHR all omit it, which is what blunts classic CSRF while keeping normal inbound links logged in.
query.title: SameSite=Lax only rides safe top-level navigations

questions.prompt: Is this Set-Cookie header stored by a modern browser over HTTPS?
questions.code: Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/; SameSite=None

query.explanation: Opting a cookie into cross-site sending with SameSite=None also requires the Secure attribute. Browsers reject the whole Set-Cookie header when SameSite=None appears without Secure, so the cookie is not stored at all (rather than silently falling back to Lax).
query.title: SameSite=None requires Secure

questions.rationale: SameSite=None is only honoured together with Secure; a None cookie without Secure is rejected outright, so it is never stored even on an HTTPS response.

questions.prompt: Is this cookie already expired at the moment it is stored?
questions.code: Set-Cookie: s=1; Path=/; Expires=Fri, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0

query.explanation: When a Set-Cookie header carries both Max-Age and Expires, the Max-Age attribute wins. Max-Age=0 (or any non-positive value) yields an expiry time at or before the current time, which is the standard way to delete a cookie, so the future Expires value has no effect.
query.title: Max-Age overrides Expires

questions.rationale: Max-Age takes precedence over Expires, and Max-Age=0 sets an expiry time in the past, so the future Expires date is ignored and the cookie is dropped immediately.

questions.prompt: Which of these cookies can document.cookie read on https://shop.example/account?

choices.rationale: HttpOnly cookies are withheld from script, so sid never appears in document.cookie.
Path=/admin does not path-match /account, so this cookie is out of scope for the current page.
Domain=other.example does not domain-match shop.example, so the browser rejects the cookie when it is set.
Correct: Secure only requires a secure channel, and the page is served over HTTPS.

Set-Cookie: sid=1; Path=/; HttpOnly
Set-Cookie: panel=2; Path=/admin
Set-Cookie: tracker=3; Path=/; Domain=other.example
Set-Cookie: theme=4; Path=/; Secure

HttpOnly hides sid from script, Path=/admin excludes panel on /account, and Domain=other.example is rejected because it is not a domain-match for shop.example. Secure is satisfied on an HTTPS page, so theme is the only readable cookie.

questions.prompt: Does this fetch send a CORS preflight before the POST?

query.title: Simple requests vs preflight

questions.rationale: text/plain is one of the three CORS-safelisted Content-Type values, so this POST is a simple request and goes out directly with an Origin header.

questions.prompt: How many of these requests trigger a CORS preflight?

choices.rationale: Only the first request is simple; the other three each break a different safelist rule.
Three requests fail: PUT is not a safelisted method, application/json is not a safelisted Content-Type, and X-Request-Id is not a safelisted header.
The GET carrying only Accept-Language is a simple request, since Accept-Language is CORS-safelisted.

questions.prompt: Which Access-Control-Allow-Origin value lets this fetch succeed?

choices.rationale: The wildcard is rejected outright when the request mode carries credentials; the header must name a single origin.
A serialized origin has no trailing slash, so this string does not match the request's Origin value byte for byte.
"null" only matches requests whose origin is opaque; this page has a real origin of https://app.example.

query.title: Credentialed requests reject the wildcard

questions.prompt: Which response header can script read with no Access-Control-Expose-Headers?

choices.rationale: ETag is not on the CORS-safelisted response header list, so it stays hidden until the server exposes it.
Set-Cookie is a forbidden response header name and is never readable from script, even if exposed.
Custom headers are invisible to cross-origin script unless named in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

const res = await fetch('https://api.example/data'); // cross-origin, no Expose-Headers
res.headers.get('???');

query.title: CORS-safelisted response headers

questions.prompt: Does this preflight response allow every header the request asked for?

query.explanation: The browser lowercases and compares header names case-insensitively, so differing casing between Access-Control-Request-Headers and Access-Control-Allow-Headers is irrelevant. Both requested names appear in the allow list.
query.title: Access-Control-Allow-Headers matching

questions.rationale: HTTP header names are case-insensitive, so x-token covers X-Token and Content-Type covers content-type; the casing difference does not fail the preflight.

questions.prompt: Which of these URLs is cross-origin to the page at https://app.example?

choices.rationale: Port 443 is the default for https, so the serialized origin is still https://app.example.
Path is not part of an origin; scheme, host and port all match.
The query string plays no part in origin comparison, so this URL is same-origin.

questions.code: const page = 'https://app.example';

query.explanation: An origin is scheme, host and port. Paths and queries are ignored, and the default port 443 serializes away for https, so only the explicit :8443 URL has a different origin.
query.title: Origin comparison for CORS

questions.prompt: Which of these attempts does this CORS config allow?

choices.rationale: An explicit non-default port makes this a different origin, so it is not in allowedOrigins.
The origin is allowed, but DELETE is absent from allowedMethods, so the preflight fails.
The scheme is part of the origin, so http://app.example does not match the https entry.

questions.prompt: Does the second requester get an Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming another origin?

query.explanation: When a server reflects the request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin it must also send Vary: Origin. Otherwise a shared cache keyed only on URL serves one origin's header to every other origin, breaking (or leaking) responses.
query.title: Why reflected origins need Vary: Origin

questions.rationale: With no Vary: Origin the shared cache reuses the first entry, so https://b.example receives the header reflecting https://a.example and the browser blocks the read.

questions.prompt: How many preflight requests does the browser send for these four requests?

choices.rationale: The cache entry made at t=0 expires at t=5, so the request at t=6 cannot reuse it.
The fresh entry created at t=6 is still valid at t=10, so that request reuses it.
Access-Control-Max-Age caches the preflight result, so the requests at t=3 and t=10 send no OPTIONS.

query.explanation: Access-Control-Max-Age: 5 caches the preflight result for 5 seconds per method/URL. t=0 preflights (valid to t=5), t=3 reuses it, t=6 preflights again (valid to t=11), t=10 reuses that entry: two OPTIONS total.
query.title: Preflight result cache

questions.prompt: What Access-Control-Allow-Origin value does this handler return here?

choices.rationale: The handler reflects the request's own Origin value, not the allow-list entry it matched against.
startsWith succeeds on this origin, so the guard passes and no null is returned.
The handler never emits a wildcard; it only reflects the incoming Origin or returns null.

questions.prompt: Which parent origin may frame a page served with this response header?

choices.rationale: The source has no '*.' wildcard, so subdomains such as www.shop.example are not covered.
The source fixes the scheme to https; an http parent does not match (only http sources upgrade to https, not the reverse).
A source without a port implies the scheme's default port 443, so port 8443 does not match.

questions.code: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://shop.example

query.explanation: A host-source with no port and an explicit scheme matches only that exact scheme, host, and the scheme's default port. 'https://shop.example' therefore matches only https://shop.example:443; a different host label (www.), a different scheme (http), or an explicit non-default port (8443) all fail to match, and the browser refuses to render the page in that frame.
query.title: frame-ancestors host-source matching

questions.prompt: What line does this code print on a top-level document?

choices.rationale: window.top equals window.self on a top-level page, so framed is false and 'bust' is never printed.
window.parent of an unframed page is the window itself, which is also window.top, so the comparison is true.
Both parts are wrong: the page is not framed, and parent and top are the same object.

questions.code:
const framed = window.top !== window.self;
console.log(framed ? 'bust' : 'ok', window.parent === window.top);

query.explanation: In a top-level browsing context window.self, window.top and window.parent all reference the same window object, so the framed test is false and the parent/top comparison is true. The guard only reports 'bust' when the document really has an ancestor frame.
query.title: top, self and parent on an unframed page

questions.prompt: Which directive stops every site, including the page's own origin, from framing it?

choices.rationale: 'self' still permits same-origin pages to frame the response, so framing is not blocked for every site.
frame-src limits which documents this page may embed; it says nothing about who may embed this page.
The CSP sandbox directive applies sandbox restrictions to the response itself; it does not prevent other pages from framing it.

query.explanation: Only frame-ancestors governs who may embed the response, and 'none' rejects all ancestors including same-origin ones. 'self' still allows same-origin framing, frame-src limits what the page itself may embed, and sandbox restricts a frame's capabilities rather than blocking embedding.
query.title: Choosing the directive that controls embedding

questions.prompt: Which directive decides whether this iframe load is allowed?

choices.rationale: frame-src is not declared in this policy, so the check falls through to the next directive in the chain.
default-src is only consulted when both frame-src and child-src are missing, and child-src is present here.
frame-ancestors restricts who may embed this page, not which documents the page may load into frames.

questions.code: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; child-src https://cdn.example

query.explanation: Iframe loads are checked against frame-src; if it is absent the check falls back to child-src, and only if that is also absent to default-src. Here child-src is present, so it governs the load and default-src is never consulted for the frame.
query.title: frame-src fallback chain

questions.prompt: How many of these parent origins does the policy below block?

choices.rationale: Only one parent is allowed, not blocked: the http variant, the non-default port and the subdomain all fail to match.
Three parents fail: http://app.example, https://partner.example:8443 and https://sub.partner.example.
https://app.example matches 'self' exactly, so it is allowed and not every parent is blocked.

questions.code:
Page origin: https://app.example
CSP: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example

Parents: https://app.example
         http://app.example
         https://partner.example:8443
         https://sub.partner.example

query.explanation: 'self' matches only the page's own origin https://app.example, so the http variant fails. The host-source https://partner.example implies default port 443, so :8443 fails, and without a '*.' wildcard sub.partner.example fails too. Exactly one parent matches and three are blocked.
query.title: Counting frame-ancestors matches

questions.prompt: Which sandbox value lets a framed same-origin page script its parent and remove the sandbox?

choices.rationale: Without allow-same-origin the frame gets an opaque origin, so its script cannot touch parent.document even though the parent is on the same site.
The frame keeps its real origin but cannot run any script, so nothing inside it can reach the parent DOM.
Neither token enables scripting or restores the origin, so the framed document still cannot execute code.

questions.code:
<!-- page and frame are both https://app.example -->
<iframe src="/widget" SANDBOX_VALUE></iframe>

<!-- candidates -->
sandbox="allow-scripts"
sandbox="allow-same-origin"
sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"
sandbox="allow-forms allow-popups"

query.explanation: Granting both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin to a frame from your own origin lets the framed script reach parent.document, rewrite the iframe's sandbox attribute, and reload itself unsandboxed. The two tokens are safe only when the framed content comes from a different origin than the framing page.
query.title: allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin defeats sandboxing

questions.prompt: does this header stop https://evil.example from framing the page in a current browser?
questions.code:
GET https://app.example/account

X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://partner.example

query.explanation: Only DENY and SAMEORIGIN are honoured by current browsers. ALLOW-FROM was never implemented in Chrome and was removed from Firefox, so the header parses as an invalid value and is discarded, leaving the page framable by any site. Use Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors to allowlist specific parents.
query.title: ALLOW-FROM is a dead X-Frame-Options value

questions.rationale: Answering True assumes ALLOW-FROM is enforced, but current browsers ignore that value entirely, so no framing restriction is applied at all.

questions.prompt: With both headers set, which parent origin can frame this page?

choices.rationale: frame-ancestors does not list 'self', and a browser that supports frame-ancestors ignores X-Frame-Options, so the page's own origin is blocked.
The two headers are not combined: frame-ancestors replaces X-Frame-Options, so SAMEORIGIN contributes nothing.
frame-ancestors names one allowed source, so framing is restricted rather than fully denied.

questions.code:
GET https://app.example/account

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://partner.example

// candidate parents: https://app.example, https://partner.example, https://evil.example

query.explanation: When a response carries both headers, browsers that implement CSP frame-ancestors use only the CSP directive and ignore X-Frame-Options; the two are never intersected. Here the single allowed parent is https://partner.example, and even the page's own origin cannot frame it unless 'self' is added to the directive.
query.title: frame-ancestors overrides X-Frame-Options

questions.prompt: does the top window navigate when this framed script assigns to top.location?
questions.code:
<!-- parent page -->
<iframe src="/widget" sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"></iframe>

<!-- inside /widget -->
<script>top.location = 'https://evil.example/';</script>

query.explanation: A sandboxed iframe loses top-level navigation unless the sandbox list includes allow-top-navigation (or allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation, which additionally requires a user gesture). With only allow-scripts and allow-forms, assigning to top.location throws a SecurityError and the top document stays put.
query.title: Sandboxed frames cannot retarget the top window

questions.rationale: Answering True assumes scripting implies navigation rights, but allow-scripts does not restore top-level navigation; that needs an explicit allow-top-navigation token.

questions.prompt: Which ancestor chain loads the page under this policy?

choices.rationale: Every ancestor is checked, and the immediate parent https://mid.example is not in the source list, so the load is blocked.
The immediate parent matches, but the top-level ancestor https://evil.example does not, and frame-ancestors validates the whole chain.
https://mid.example is not an allowed source, so this single-level framing is refused.

questions.code:
// response for the innermost page
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://outer.example

// chains are listed outermost first
1) https://outer.example -> page
2) https://outer.example -> https://mid.example -> page
3) https://evil.example -> https://outer.example -> page
4) https://mid.example -> page

query.explanation: frame-ancestors is evaluated against each ancestor browsing context, not just the immediate parent. A nested chain loads only if every ancestor origin matches a listed source, which is why an allowed parent wrapped inside an unlisted top-level page is still blocked.
query.title: frame-ancestors checks every ancestor

choices.rationale: 'beforebegin' on the span inserts before the span, not at the end of d, so <u>3</u> cannot be the last child.
1 was inserted with 'afterbegin' on d and stays d's first child; 3 only has to precede the span, not the .
'afterend' places 2 after the span as a following sibling, so the span still comes before the .

questions.prompt: What HTML does this code log?

query.explanation: insertAdjacentHTML is an HTML-parsing sink just like innerHTML, so auditing it means knowing exactly where attacker markup lands. The position is relative to the element the method is called on: 'afterbegin' puts the fragment as that element's first child, 'beforeend' as its last child, while 'beforebegin' and 'afterend' insert it as a sibling in the parent. Here the first call targets d, so 1 becomes d's first child: [b, span]. The next two calls target the span, so 2 lands after the span and 3 lands immediately before it, giving 13x2. Because every one of these positions runs the HTML parser, a payload such as would execute from any of them, which is why position does not change exploitability — only where the injected node ends up in the tree.
query.title: insertAdjacentHTML position semantics

choices.rationale: That would need all three on* attributes gone; the forward index loop skips one handler after each removal.
The loop does remove attributes: onclick and onfocus are both stripped, so the original five cannot all survive.
Only names beginning with 'on' are candidates for removal, so id and href are never touched.

questions.prompt: How many attributes remain on the anchor after this loop runs?

query.explanation: element.attributes is a live NamedNodeMap, so removing an attribute shifts every later entry down one index while the loop counter still moves forward. Starting order is id, onclick, onmouseover, onfocus, href. At i=1 onclick is removed, so onmouseover slides into index 1 and is never inspected; i=2 now sees onfocus and removes it. The loop ends with id, onmouseover and href still attached, leaving a live event handler on supposedly sanitized markup. Safe sanitizers snapshot the names first (Array.from(el.attributes).map(a => a.name)) or iterate backwards.
query.title: Live attribute maps break index loops

choices.rationale: For special schemes the WHATWG parser maps backslashes onto slashes, so the target is read as protocol-relative and the host comes from the input rather than the base.
The host property never contains path data; it is only host plus optional port.
The string parses fine against a base URL, so no TypeError occurs.

questions.prompt: What host does this code log?

query.explanation: A naive guard that only rejects targets starting with "//" misses "/\\/host". When resolving against an http(s) base, the URL parser treats "\" exactly like "/" for special schemes, so "/\\/evil.example/path" goes through relative-slash and special-authority states and parses evil.example as the authority. The redirect leaves the site even though the raw string begins with a single "/". Safe checks resolve the target with new URL(next, base) first and then compare url.host (or url.origin) against an allowlist, instead of inspecting the raw string prefix.
query.title: Backslashes make a path look protocol-relative

choices.rationale: An exact match between request path and cookie path always path-matches.
The cookie path is a prefix and the next character of the request path is '/', so it path-matches.
The cookie path is a prefix and the first unmatched character is '/', so deeper paths under /admin path-match.
Prefix matching is not plain string prefixing: the character after '/admin' is 't', not '/', so this path does not match.

questions.code:
Set-Cookie: sid=1; Path=/admin

Candidate request paths:
  /admin
  /admin/
  /admin/settings/edit
  /administrator/panel
questions.prompt: Which of these request paths does this cookie not get sent to?

query.explanation: RFC 6265 path-match holds when the request path equals the cookie path, or the cookie path is a prefix of it and either the cookie path ends in '/' or the first character of the request path not covered by the prefix is '/'. '/administrator/panel' starts with the characters '/admin' but the next character is 't', so it is a different path segment and the cookie is not sent. The other three paths are either equal to /admin or sit beneath it as real segments.
query.title: Cookie path matching is segment-based, not string-prefix-based
